newsitem.title: USA: NY gambles tax revenues in bid to help retailers.
newsitem.headline: NY gambles tax revenues in bid to help retailers.

text.p: Attention New York shoppers -- state officials want you to shop 'til you drop.

New York state is lifting its 4 percent sales tax on clothing priced below $500 for one week beginning on Friday, risking $20 million in revenue to determine how much the tax harms retailers, officials said in a statement.

The plan's purpose is actually twofold, state officials said. It may keep New Yorkers from making shopping trips to nearby New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Connecticut -- states with lower or no tax on clothing -- which would help New York's economy and give shoppers a break.
Plus, some officials said, the New York tax is unfair because clothes are a neccessity. Other necessities such as food and drugs are not subject to sales tax in New York.

With most cities and towns matching the state's offer, shoppers in New York stand to save up to 8.50 percent on clothing and shoes. Officials said they will be watching whether that extra money is saved or spent on other items.
If the one-week experiment is successful, state officials may try to eliminate the sales tax on clothing altogether.
The yearly loss is estimated at $700 million -- only part of which might be recouped by higher taxes businesses will pay on higher income as profits inevitably increase.

State officials admit eliminating the tax will force further budget cuts to compensate for lost revenues. But retailers, many of whom have complained for years that the tax on clothes forces shoppers out of New York, are thrilled.

"It is long overdue," Walter Eisenhardt, store manager of Barneys New York in the World Financial Center, said. "It is giving New Yorkers the opportunity to enjoy the same tax free purchases as someone in New Jersey has been able to enjoy all these years."
Yet some were perplexed as to why the state decided to experiment with the sales tax in mid-January -- traditionally a slow period for sales -- rather than during the holiday shopping season.
State officials said the original proposal was to have the tax-free week in December, but it was decided the loss to the state would have been too great.
New Jersey officials conceded that the one week tax cut may curtail sales a bit, but said they were not worried.

"While New York will do no tax on clothing for one week, New Jersey for 52 weeks out of the year has no tax on clothing, drugs, utilities or fuel and food, among several other items," Lisa Kruse, spokeswoman for the New Jersey Department of Commerce said. "We think shoppers will remember who is tax free all year long."
